## Discussion

By re-analyzing reads typically discarded by transcriptomic pipelines, we show that cutaneous HPV is active in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and quiet in healthy skin. In cSCC and actinic keratosis, it appears only as a trace amount, a presence that increased sequencing depth or improved library chemistry cannot turn into a productive infection.

Against the prior RNA-seq and in situ reports of silence in cutaneous carcinoma (Introduction), our study adds rigorous controls, a clear denominator, and a defined metric. While past work evaluated 11 to 345 specimens, we jointly analyze `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK libraries and `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries in one pipeline. This turns an absence report into a case-control comparison with an effect size. We score productive replication, not just presence, against a baseline of confirmed productive lesions: the same instrument that finds no productive infection in cSCC/AK reports `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% productivity in warts.

This result does not settle the mechanism, because all three models predict a declining viral signal along the progression axis. The hit-and-run model works because a genome that nothing selects for is lost from the expanding clone, dispensability being what permits that loss rather than what causes it [@you2004]. Protective immunity works because virus-positive cells face negative selection [@strickley2019; @son2025]. Cis-restriction works because quiescence is the viral default [@rehm2022]. A fourth consideration is not a model but a property of the readout: late transcription requires terminal differentiation [@doorbar2012], so a poorly differentiated tumor cannot run the late program regardless. Our trace decomposition answers it, since `r tr("trace_pct_nogene")`% of below-floor skin and neoplasia libraries carry no reads on any HPV gene at all, not merely no late ones (@suppfig-trace). Our data measure this exact axis and cannot separate the three models. Nor does absent transcription imply clearance: episomal genomes may persist silently, or with intermittent activity, below the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. Likewise, absent productive transcription in established lesions does not exclude a transient viral contribution earlier in carcinogenesis.

The elevated beta-HPV activity that Son and colleagues found in keratinocyte clones of sun-exposed skin [@son2025] does not conflict with our quiet reservoir, because we sequenced whole biopsies without sorting for ultraviolet exposure. A signal arising from small keratinocyte clones is diluted when averaged across an entire biopsy, a documented effect for cutaneous HPV [@purdie2005]. The same logic applies to the HPV8-driven expansion of Lrig1⁺ follicular stem cells in actinic keratosis [@morgan2024]. We nevertheless agree on viral presence: we recovered trace HPV from `r pp(stats$ak_pctany)`% of AK libraries. HPV8 itself, however, was absent at any level from all `r comma(rvn("n_rna_all"))` analyzed RNA libraries. That absence argues against persistent productive HPV8 transcription in established lesions while remaining compatible with transient, focal or latent activity. An E6-driven stem cell mechanism requires oncogene function, not capsid production, which matches our non-productive footprint. The nine-valent vaccine reduced the burden of actinic keratosis in a randomized trial [@wenande2025]. It targets mucosal alpha types, not the resident beta reservoir, so any protective effect likely depends on cross-reactive or non-specific immunity.

The rare productive infections we do find are beta-HPV, which constrains how the trace result should be read. Outside warts and EV, three primary-skin lesions carry unambiguous productive infection: an HPV12-productive cSCC, and two actinic-keratosis/cSCC libraries co-infected with HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These are Betapapillomavirus 1, 5 and 2 respectively, so the genus running a complete productive program in these lesions is the same genus the cofactor debate concerns. Productive beta-HPV infection of primary skin is therefore possible and simply rare. The silence we report in cutaneous neoplasia is thus not a ceiling on what beta-HPV can do in skin. No productive HPV12, HPV96 or HPV182 has to our knowledge been described from public RNA-seq of primary skin.

A 2–4% active transcription rate does not contradict a 90% viral DNA reservoir. Three factors reconcile this gap. First, beta-HPV DNA loads sit below one copy per 60 cells [@weissenborn2012], falling beneath the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. Second, the tissue sources differ: skin epidemiology studies test surface swabs and hair bulbs (92% and 73% prevalence) [@rollison2019sites], while RNA-seq uses deep biopsies that miss surface and hair follicle layers. Third, screening panels miss 229 skin types that lack reference genomes [@bzhalava2014]. Ultimately, our figure reflects the actively transcribed portion of a widespread reservoir. DNA data confirms that the general reservoir differs from tumor-driving viruses: fewer than 5% of skin types match later cSCC [@rollison2021], and paired eyebrow hair and cSCC showed only 9.1% genotype concordance in another cohort [@oh2026].

Unadjusted analyses are dominated by contamination. Cultured materials show a five-fold enrichment that reflects known HeLa cell contamination in archives [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], traced in one facility to a quality-control cell pool run with tumors [@selitsky2020]. Furthermore, over 65% of viral sequences from 712 libraries group with reagents or protocols instead of actual specimens [@asplund2019], and re-analyses have invalidated major archive-scale microbial findings [@gihawi2023]. While our safeguards are not individually new [@cantalupo2019], our contribution lies in operationalizing them by quantifying the size of each artifact rather than merely asserting it.

While petabase-scale surveys are now the standard method for establishing viral presence across body sites, a presence catalog cannot measure biological activity. Because these surveys rely on sequence assembly, integrated genomes fail to assemble across the virus-host junction. Consequently, the viral genome state must be inferred from individual reads or transcription rather than catalog membership alone. For example, conditioning data on near-complete L1-anchored contigs yields an intact E2 gene in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs compared to 99.9% in skin (@supptbl-e2). This finding approaches a tautology, as the completeness criterion itself inherently selects for episomal genomes in both tissues.

Several limitations affect these findings, starting with the non-random nature of archival sampling, which makes the absolute healthy-skin rate an estimate. Furthermore, sequencing chemistry could only be resolved for `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of libraries, while input amount, RNA integrity, and fragment selection are entirely unrecoverable from the archived metadata. Because a biopsy average dilutes focal transcription (above), our productivity estimates are a conservative lower bound. Finally, because tissue and diagnosis labels are programmatic and imperfect, viral typing is constrained by the reference panel, and the data are cross-sectional, these results describe productive-status phenomenology rather than prove a definitive mechanism.

Ultimately, cutaneous HPV is productive in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis, but leaves only a trace, non-productive footprint in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, regardless of sequencing depth or library chemistry. This distinct phenotype forms the fundamental baseline that any current theory of beta-HPV in skin cancer must address. Because all major hypotheses predict this outcome, more precise measurement of viral activity will not separate them. That requires study designs that break the shared prediction. Crucial approaches include matched DNA and RNA profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, precise spatial resolution of residual viral particles relative to mutant clones and infiltrating T cells, and ongoing interventional studies. While single-cell resolution has already been demonstrated in cutaneous lesions [@devitt2019], the critical next step is applying this technology at a cohort scale across the actinic-keratosis-to-carcinoma transition.
